subject: Model consultation for linear mixed effects: Stan mixing really poorly

messages.author: 395bdca538bcae5d
messages.subject: Model consultation for linear mixed effects: Stan mixing really poorly
parts:
I'm wondering if someone can give me some advice for improving mixing for a model.

I'm trying to recreate an analysis from a paper that used the R package glmmMCMC to analyse a fairly complex linear mixed effects model. The model is from quantitative genetics and was analyzed as example 4 in this study: http://icesjms.oxfordjournals.org/content/early/2014/12/03/icesjms.fsu213.abstract

Here is the R formula version of the model:
body_weight ~ Reciprocal_Cross + degree_days_centered, random =
              ~animal + Dam + Tank_ID + ID

There are 1338 observations (rows). There are 15 fixed effects (Reciprocal_Cross and degree_days_centered) including 5 variance terms. The random effect sizes are: 1338 for animal, 183 for Dam, 57 for Tank_ID and 39 for ID. The whole point is the partition the variance.

I tried fitting this in Stan and JAGS, and found that JAGS was significantly faster for both the centered and non-centered ('.nc') versions of the model.

Here's a quick table from runs with 20,000 iterations and adapt_delta=0.9:

stan jags stan.nc jags.nc
time 1269.7 94.87 3140.25 154.34
minESS 12.3912 11.1872 24.2888 13.0488
minESS/time 0.0098 0.1179 0.0077 0.0845

The hypervariance controlling the animal random effects, which there is one for each observation, is the bottleneck here, although both Stan and JAGS seem to struggle with multiple parameters (see attached plot which shows ordered ESS for the 4 models).

I've been working through Michael's paper on hierarchical models for HMC (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.0906.pdf) and understand the implications for hypervariances with so much influence on the log posterior and the issues that arise from it. However, short of using RMHMC, I'm not sure how to "fix" it.

Presumably I could try to rewrite the likelihood statement to be in matrix notation, but that wouldn't affect the mixing only the time per transition. Is this type of model just really tough for HMC in it's current state? Is this a model we would expect JAGS to do better b/c it's a linear mixed effects model? (BTW JAGS is using slice sampling for variances and "glm::Albert-Chib" for everything else).

I've attached data, model files, and an R script to recreate the table and attached figure.

Thanks ahead of time,
Cole

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model consultation for linear mixed effects: Stan mixing really poorly
parts:
Hi, you don’t want this real<lower=0,upper=10> stuff.  Instead just do real<lower=0> and put informative priors on these scale parameters, for example normal(0,1).  You are doing t_2(0,1) which could be ok—I don’t know enough about our example—but these long tails may not be needed.

SImilarly for a and b, don’t do normal(0,1e5), do something like normal(0,1) or normal(0,10).  In this case you should probably do normal(A,B) with weak priors on A and B.  No need to let the parameters completely float, that’s just asking for trouble.

Also no need for all those square roots, you can just parametrize scale paraemters directly.

Another thing is that you might want to center your linear predictor (“days”); if it is far from 0, this can give you big posterior correlations.

Also, have you tried simply fitting the model in rstanarm?  I’m curious how that would work for this example.

This is definitely the sort of example that we _don’t_ want Stan to have trouble with!

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model consultation for linear mixed effects: Stan mixing really poorly
parts:
The real problem here is that neither Stan nor JAGS are able
to fit your model as specified.

When you have 10K iterations and n_eff values of 10,
it means something's not working.

If you look at the posterior for ua_raw, you'll see
that it's just noise (sd >> absolut effect size).
If you look at the pairs plot for the parameters that have
10 draws,

> pairs(fit, pars=c("sa", "se")

you see a highly correlated banana shape, which poses
problems for MCMC.

If you remove ua_raw and sa, Stan's default settings work very
well with random inits (fits in 15s/chain, all Rhat under 1.01,
minimum n_eff > 200, etc.)

I'm attaching a recoded mostly non-centered parameterization
and the script to run it (data was in the original post).

You'll see that I vectorized the ypred calculation and
made the prior changes that Andrew suggested. I also standardized
both the outcome (body weight) and the fixed effect (days).
I doubt any of these changes is critical --- the real issue is
that sa was just noise.

I left the pieces I removed commented out. I figured since
n_animal = 1500, that a centered parameterization would work better
there. But in fact, it didn't help at all.

I am curious why this isn't fitting with the extra random effect,
even if it is noise.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model consultation for linear mixed effects: Stan mixing really poorly
parts:
> The real problem here is that neither Stan nor JAGS are able
> to fit your model as specified.
>
> When you have 10K iterations and n_eff values of 10,
> it means something's not working.

We only ever have _estimates_ for the effective sample size,
and those estimators are notoriously finicky. In particular, if
n_eff / n_transitions < 0.001 then there is no way that you have
enough information in your chains to construct a reasonable
n_eff estimate.

Immediately this invalidates your quantitative results, as you’re
comparing the small n_eff which is the most susceptible to bias
(let alone noise) The n_eff plots demonstrate this clearly —
Stan is sampling far more parameters reasonably well than
JAGS, although even this should be interpreted carefully given
the interval of vanishing n_eff. If _any_ of the parameters have
low n_eff then you have to consider that all of the other parameters
are sampling not from the joint distribution but rather the conditional
distribution with those low n_eff parameters essentially set to constants.

This is why comparisons to JAGS are so hard — the JAGS samplers
are really hard to diagnose and end up taking a huge amount of time
to verify. Whereas when HMC hits problems it makes that clear immediately.
I won’t even get into how frustrating it is trying to recreate published
analyses that blindly trust fits out of packages like glmmMCMC...

As Andy notes, get rid of the sqrts and just model the deviations
directly. Don’t use uniform priors and instead stick to soft
constraints.

As Bob notes, any strong nonlinearity in the model is a potential
cause of sampling problems. Because there’s only one slope,
standardizing days (or body weight for that matter) won’t have
a huge effect. There is however, an immediate problems
with your model.

There’s no global mean for all the ypred. If <ypred> isn’t
zero then this forces the distribution of random effects to be
biased away from zero which causes tension with the priors
(which wants them to be distributed around zero) and induces
non-identifiabilities (as there are many ways the random effects
can trade off to achieve some non-zero bias).

Also, centering a will help speed up adaptation in Stan.

parameters {
// fixed effects
real b;

// hyper variances
real<lower=0> sigma_animal;
real<lower=0> sigma_id;
real<lower=0> sigma_tank;
real<lower=0> sigma_dam;
real<lower=0> sigma;

// random effects
real alpha;
real alpha_cross_raw[n_cross];
real alpha_animal_raw[n_animal];
real alpha_id_raw[n_ID];
real alpha_tank_raw[n_Tank_ID];
real alpha_dam_raw[n_Dam];
}

model {
real ypred[N];
for(i in 1:N)
ypred[i] <- b * days[i] + alpha_cross_raw[cross[i]] * 100 + alpha
+ alpha_animal_raw[animal[i]] * sigma_animal;
+ alpha_id_raw[ID[i]] * sigma_id;
+ alpha_tank_raw[Tank_ID[i]] * sigma_tank;
+ alpha_dam_raw[Dam[i]] * sigma_dam;

// Priors:
b ~ normal(0, 100);

alpha ~ normal(0, 10);
alpha_cross ~ normal(0, 1);
alpha_animal_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
alpha_id_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
alpha_tank_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
alpha_dam_raw ~ normal(0, 1)

sigma_animal ~ student_t(2,0,1);
sigma_id ~ student_t(2,0,1);
sigma_tank ~ student_t(2,0,1);
sigma_dam ~ student_t(2,0,1);
sigma ~ student_t(2,0,1);

// likelihood
body_weight~normal(ypred, sigma);

}

> that it's just noise (sd >> absolut effect size).

> 10 draws,

>
> If you remove ua_raw and sa, Stan's default settings work very

Yes, it's a relatively new feature. The vectorization
cuts down the number of intermediate expressions in the
autodiff expression graph, so reduces the number of virtual
function calls at run time and also avoid some redundant
recalculations --- so it's a win in both time and memory.

- Bob
